title: How fiber can help lower cholesterol and improve employee heart health
summary: Learn how dietary fiber helps lower your employees' cholesterol. Explore soluble fiber, high fiber foods, and practical nutrition steps for better employee heart health.
body_markdown:
September marks Cholesterol Awareness Month, an opportune moment for employers to examine the role of nutrition in[cardiovascular risk reduction](https://www.labcorp.com/education-events/articles/three-healthy-habits-fight-cardiovascular-disease) .[Cholesterol](https://www.heart.org/en/health-topics/cholesterol/about-cholesterol) is a fat-like, waxy substance present in every cell of the body.


The liver produces sufficient cholesterol to build cells, synthesize sex hormones, and generate vitamin D, while additional cholesterol is absorbed from animal-based foods. Cholesterol is essential for health, but having too much low-density lipoprotein (LDL), often called "bad" cholesterol, increases the risk of heart disease and stroke.


The[Centers for Disease Control and Prevention](https://www.cdc.gov/cholesterol/about/index.html) (CDC) states the optimal levels for most adults are a total cholesterol below 200 mg/dL, LDL below 100 mg/dL, HDL at least 40 mg/dL for men and 50 mg/dL for women, and triglycerides below 150 mg/dL. For[individuals 19 and younger](https://medlineplus.gov/cholesterollevelswhatyouneedtoknow.html) , total cholesterol should remain below 170 mg/dL and LDL below 110 mg/dL. Risk escalates with age, and high total cholesterol is most prevalent among adults aged 40-59.


## The biological mechanism: How soluble fiber lowers cholesterol


[Soluble fiber](https://www.ucsfhealth.org/health-articles/increasing-fiber-intake) is the operative component behind fiber's cholesterol-lowering efficacy. Because it’s not absorbed in the intestine, soluble fiber dissolves in water to form a viscous gel that binds to bile acids (which are composed of cholesterol) in the digestive tract, preventing their reabsorption and facilitating their excretion.


When bile acids are lost, the liver draws cholesterol from circulating blood to synthesize replacement bile, a process that upregulates hepatic LDL receptors and increases clearance of LDL cholesterol. The[clinical effect is measurable](https://www.medicalnewstoday.com/articles/does-soluble-fat-bind-cholesterol#intake) as consuming 5 to 10 grams of soluble fiber daily can lower total and LDL cholesterol by 5 to 11 points.


## Soluble vs. insoluble fiber


Dietary fiber comprises two functional types. Soluble fiber dissolves in water to form a gel and is concentrated in oats, barley, legumes, and the flesh of fruits and vegetables, It stabilizes blood glucose, lowers cholesterol, and supports weight management.


Insoluble fiber doesn’t dissolve, it:


- Adds bulk to stool
- Promotes regularity
- Is concentrated in whole grains, wheat bran, and vegetable skins


Most plant foods contain a mixture of both, but because soluble fiber is the type that binds bile acids, it’s the focus of any cholesterol-lowering strategy. This distinction explains why the foods highlighted below were selected over other fiber-rich options.


## Recommended fiber intake and safe implementation


The appropriate amount of dietary fiber is 14 grams per 1,000 calories, approximately 25 grams per day for women and 38 grams per day for men. Roughly 25%-33% of intake should be soluble fiber.


To increase fiber safely, employees should gradually increase their fiber intake over several weeks accompanied by adequate hydration, which facilitates transit through the digestive tract and minimizes gastrointestinal discomfort.


## Foods and drinks that reduce cholesterol


Several foods and beverages lower LDL efficiently when substituted for less healthy options.


The following selections were chosen for their soluble-fiber density:


- **Vegetables:** Brussels sprouts (2.0 g soluble fiber per ½ cup), sweet potatoes (1.8 g), and turnips (1.7 g) also deliver vitamins A, C, and K alongside anti-inflammatory, vision, gut, and immune system health benefits
- **Grains:** Barley (0.8-2.2 g per ½ cup) and oats (1.9 g per cup) supply beta-glucan, the soluble fiber most strongly associated with LDL reduction. Barley is a chewy grain, like oats. In fact, you can cook and enjoy barley in the same way you would oats, including as a hot morning cereal. Rye is another grain than reduces cholesterol. Its kernels are called rye berries and can be cooked or mixed into dishes, such as warm salads and hearty vegetable-based dishes
- **Fruits:** Oranges, pears, apricots, apples, and passion fruit provide 1.5-2.0 g of soluble fiber per serving. They also contain important nutrients, support digestive and heart health (potassium-rich fruits may help reduce blood pressure), provide a source of hydration, and promote optimal immune system function
- **Seeds:** Chia and flaxseeds combine soluble fiber with heart-healthy omega-3 fats. You can sprinkle them on virtually anything, including yogurt


Additional high-fiber foods include lentils, peas, whole grains, berries, and avocados. Green tea and soluble-fiber-rich legumes provide further, albeit modest, benefits.


## Foods most detrimental to cholesterol management


Saturated and trans fats are the primary dietary drivers of elevated LDL cholesterol. The American Heart Association recommends limiting saturated fat to[less than 6% of total calories](https://www.heart.org/en/healthy-living/healthy-eating/eat-smart/fats/saturated-fats) .


The most detrimental choices include red meat, full-fat dairy, butter, fried foods, processed meats, commercial baked goods, and tropical oils. Replacing saturated fats with unsaturated alternatives such as olive oil, avocados, nuts, and fatty fish such as salmon can also help lower LDL while raising HDL.


## Complementary diet and lifestyle modifications


Fiber achieves its greatest effect as part of a comprehensive strategy. Replacing saturated fats with unsaturated fats, consuming fatty fish twice weekly, maintaining a healthy weight, engaging in regular physical activity, limiting alcohol, and avoiding tobacco can independently improve lipid levels.


By equipping employees with this framework, organizations can meaningfully advance workforce cardiovascular health.
